title: Type coercion and language edge cases
summary: How objects become primitives, the steps of ==, NaN and -0, and coercion in + and comparisons.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up which of valueOf and toString is tried first for a hint, or believes + and templates both use the same one.
Believes an object turns into the same primitive in every conversion, whatever the operation asks for.
Believes valueOf may return an object or array and the result is still used as the value.
Believes == compares truthiness, so an empty array is not equal to false or null equals false.
Believes == on two objects compares their contents or their converted values.
Checks for missing values with === null, which misses undefined, or with a truthiness test, which also catches 0.
Believes NaN equals NaN in every comparison, so indexOf finds it, or that includes cannot.
Believes === can tell -0 from 0, or that JavaScript replaces -0 with 0.
Believes decimal sums such as 0.1 + 0.2 are exact, so == or toFixed fixes the comparison.
Believes sort with no function orders numbers by value.
Believes < compares as text whenever one side is text, instead of converting to numbers.
Believes + adds all numbers first or joins everything once a string appears, and that brackets do not matter.

conceptCard.title: How objects become primitives
conceptCard.body: An object turns into a primitive with a hint: default, number or string. The default and number hints call valueOf first, and the string hint calls toString first. A Symbol.toPrimitive method replaces both and receives the hint.

conceptCard.title: The steps of ==
conceptCard.body: == compares same types like ===. For different types it converts: null equals only undefined, a boolean becomes a number, and an object becomes a primitive when the other side is a primitive. Two objects are equal only if they are the same object.

conceptCard.title: NaN, -0, Infinity and floating point
conceptCard.body: NaN is the only value not strictly equal to itself, so use Number.isNaN. A zero can have a sign: === sees -0 and 0 as equal, Object.is does not. Dividing by zero gives Infinity, and decimal sums are rounded.

conceptCard.title: Coercion in +, comparisons and sorting
conceptCard.body: + joins when one side is text and adds otherwise. - and * turn text into numbers. A comparison of a number and a text uses numbers; two texts compare by characters. Sorting with no function compares items as text.

items.prompt: A ferry fare object defines both conversion methods. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. + asks for a default conversion, which tries valueOf first. A template literal asks for text, which tries toString first.
You used toString for the +. A + with no clear type asks for the default conversion, which tries valueOf first, so the first line is a sum.
You used valueOf for the template too. A template literal wants text, so it tries toString first and uses its result.

items.explanation: The default hint, used by +, tries valueOf first: 4 + 1 is 5. The string hint, used by a template literal, tries toString first, so the second line prints ticket.
hints: Compare how the object is used on line 5 and on line 6.
An object becomes a primitive with a hint: default, number or string.
The default hint tries valueOf first; the string hint tries toString first.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A Tank class defines Symbol.toPrimitive. Which statement explains why the last line differs from the first two?

options.text: The method receives a hint, and only the template literal asks for the string hint.
options.feedback: Right. Unary plus and + ask for number and default; a template literal asks for string.

options.text: The hint is the same for every conversion, so all three lines would print the same.
options.feedback: Each operation passes its own hint. Unary plus passes number, + passes default and a template passes string.

options.text: Template literals skip the method and call toString, so the last line prints an object text.
options.feedback: Symbol.toPrimitive replaces valueOf and toString for every hint, template literals included. toString is not tried when Symbol.toPrimitive exists.

items.explanation: Symbol.toPrimitive is called with the hint. Unary plus passes number and + with a number passes default, so both get the stored 40. A template literal passes string, so the method returns T.
hints: Look at the three operations and what each one asks of tank.
Each operation tells the object which kind of primitive it wants.
Only one of the three operations asks for the string hint.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The shipping total should print 12, but prints 5 kg7 kg. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. valueOf returns a number, so + adds the two crates.
valueOf must return a primitive. An object is skipped, so + falls back to toString and joins two [object Object] texts.
An array is an object, not a primitive. + ignores it and uses toString, so the result is still joined text.

items.explanation: + uses the primitive from valueOf. Returning text makes + join the two texts. Returning the number lets + add them. A returned object is ignored and toString is used instead.
hints: Check what line 6 returns when + converts a crate.
valueOf decides the primitive a crate becomes in +.
Return only the weight.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of describeUnits(n). Build an object that becomes n for the number hint and n plus " units" otherwise. Return [+obj, `${obj}`, obj + ""].
items.explanation: The method gets the hint, so it can return n for the number hint and text for the others. A method that ignores the hint returns one kind of value for every conversion, and a plain valueOf leaves the string hint to toString, which gives '[object Object]'.
hints: Define a method under the Symbol.toPrimitive key and look at its parameter.
The parameter tells which conversion is wanted: number, string or default.
Return n when the hint is number, otherwise return the text.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A packing list is an empty array. What do these three comparisons print?

options.feedback: Right. The array becomes an empty text and then 0, equal to false as 0. null equals only undefined, so the last line is false.
You judged the array by truthiness. == does not do that: it converts the array to a primitive and both sides to numbers.
You treated null like false. null is loosely equal only to undefined, so the last comparison is false.

items.explanation: With a boolean, == turns it into a number. The array becomes "" and then 0, and false becomes 0, so line 3 is true. Line 4 compares with !slot, which is false. null == false is false.
hints: Line 3 compares an object with a boolean; line 5 involves null.
== converts a boolean to a number, then an object to a primitive.
An empty array becomes 0; null equals only undefined.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Two objects with the same valueOf result are compared with ==. Which statement explains the last line?

options.text: When both sides are objects, == compares identity and never calls valueOf.
options.feedback: Right. Converting an object happens only when the other side is a primitive.

options.text: == calls valueOf on both sides, so the last line compares 8 with 8 and is true.
options.feedback: That happens only when one side is a primitive. With two objects, == checks whether they are the very same object.

options.text: == never calls valueOf and compares text forms, so the first line is false.
options.feedback: == does call valueOf when the other side is a primitive, so the first line is true.

items.explanation: == runs the conversion steps only when one side is an object and the other a primitive. With two objects it compares references, and a and b are different objects.
hints: Compare the last line with the first two.
The steps of == depend on the types of both sides.
Look at what both sides are on the last line.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The survey should count 2 missing scores, but prints 1. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. null and undefined are loosely equal to each other and to nothing else.
=== null catches null but not undefined, so only one score is counted.
!s is also true for 0, which is a real score here, so three are counted.

items.explanation: Line 5: s == false converts false to 0, so it matches 0 but never null or undefined. s == null is true for exactly null and undefined, which is what missing means here.
hints: Check which of the four marks line 5 counts.
null is loosely equal only to undefined, not to false.
Use a comparison that matches exactly null and undefined.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A parcel weight sits in an array. Fill the blanks so both lines print true.

options.feedback: Right. The array becomes the text "5", then 5 equals 5.
true becomes 1 before the comparison, while the array becomes 5. 5 == 1 is false, so this prints false.
Right. null and undefined are loosely equal.
A second array is a different object, so == on two objects is false.
The array becomes 5, not 0, and null is not loosely equal to 0, so this prints false.
Neither side converts to an empty text that matches: the array gives "5" and null equals only undefined.

items.explanation: An array and a primitive: the array becomes a primitive text, then both sides are compared. With null, == is true only for undefined, never for numbers or text.
hints: Line 2 compares an array with a primitive; line 3 compares null.
An array becomes a text and then == compares with the other side.
The first blank is a primitive that equals the array's value after conversion; null has one partner.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A sensor log holds a NaN reading. What do these three lines print?

options.feedback: Right. indexOf compares with ===, which never matches NaN, and NaN === NaN is false. includes treats NaN as equal to itself.
You expected indexOf to find NaN. It uses ===, and NaN is not strictly equal to anything, even itself.
includes uses a different comparison from indexOf and treats NaN as equal to itself, so it finds the value.

items.explanation: indexOf uses strict equality, and NaN === NaN is false, so it returns -1. includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to NaN. Line 4 shows the strict comparison directly.
hints: Compare indexOf on line 2 with includes on line 3, and read line 4.
Array methods differ in how they compare values.
Only one of the first two methods can find NaN.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A gauge reads negative zero. Which statement explains why the first two lines disagree?

options.text: === ignores the sign of zero, while Object.is and division can tell -0 from 0.
options.feedback: Right. -0 and 0 are different numbers that === treats as equal.

options.text: === compares the sign of zero, so it is false for -0 and 0 while Object.is says they match.
options.feedback: It is the other way round. === says they are equal, and Object.is is the one that separates them.

options.text: -0 becomes 0 when it is stored, so every line behaves as if drift was 0.
options.feedback: -0 is kept as it is. If it became 0, 1 / drift would print Infinity.

items.explanation: === treats -0 and 0 as equal. Object.is compares the sign too, and dividing by -0 gives -Infinity. String turns -0 into the text 0, so printing text hides the sign.
hints: Look at lines 2 and 4 together.
A number can be zero and still carry a sign.
One comparison ignores the sign and another one keeps it.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The check should print exact, but prints nothing. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. Comparing the difference with a small tolerance accepts the tiny rounding error.
== between two numbers compares them exactly like ===. The tiny error is still there and nothing prints.
toFixed returns text, and text is never strictly equal to a number, so nothing prints.

items.explanation: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point, so === with 0.3 is false. Compare the distance from 0.3 with a small tolerance instead of testing equality.
hints: Print total to see what line 4 is really comparing.
Decimal fractions are rounded in binary, so sums can be a hair off.
Test whether the two numbers are close, not equal.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of safeRatio(a, b). Return a divided by b, or null when the result is not a finite number.
items.explanation: Dividing by zero gives Infinity or NaN, and a huge result also overflows to Infinity. Number.isFinite rejects NaN and both infinities in one check.
hints: Compute the ratio first, then test the result.
Bad results are NaN, Infinity and -Infinity.
Number.isFinite is false for all three.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A turnstile log mixes number sizes and text. What do these three lines print?

options.feedback: Right. Two texts compare character by character; a number and a text compare as numbers; sort with no function compares as text.
You compared numerically everywhere. Two texts compare by characters, and sort with no function also compares as text.
Line 3 has a number on one side, so the text becomes a number and 12 < 3 is false. Only two texts compare as text.

items.explanation: Two strings compare by character code, so "12" < "3". With a number on one side, < converts to numbers. The default sort converts items to text, so 100 and 12 come before 25 and 3.
hints: Compare the operands on lines 2 and 3.
< compares as text only when both sides are text.
The default sort treats every item as text.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A seat chart joins a seat object, a number and text with +. Which statement explains the three results?

options.text: Each + turns the object into 2, then works left to right: it adds two numbers, but joins as soon as one side is text.
options.feedback: Right. Each + decides by the two values it has at that moment.

options.text: + joins text everywhere as soon as one string appears in the expression, so line 2 prints 23x.
options.feedback: + looks at one pair at a time. seat + 3 is two numbers once seat becomes 2, so they are added before the text appears.

options.text: Brackets do not change +, so the last line prints x23.
options.feedback: Brackets run first. seat + 3 is worked out as 5 before anything is joined, and that 5 is then joined to the text.

items.explanation: Each + works on one pair, left to right, after the object becomes the primitive 2. 2 + 3 adds to 5 and then joins with the text. In the second line the text comes first, so every later value is joined. Brackets run first.
hints: Work out the pairs one + at a time on lines 2 and 3.
The object becomes a primitive first; then the type of the two values on each + decides adding or joining.
Brackets in the last line are evaluated before any joining.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The program should print the largest bay number, 75, but it prints 9. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. Unary plus turns both texts into numbers, so the comparison is numeric.
The comparison still sees two texts, so hi stays at 9. Converting after the test is too late.
This compares the number of characters, so it stops at 10 and prints 10.

items.explanation: When both sides of > are texts, they are compared character by character, so "9" is greater than "75". Converting each side to a number first makes the comparison numeric.
hints: Look at what line 4 compares.
Two texts are compared as text; a number comparison needs numbers.
Convert both sides of the comparison, not the value you store.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A depot lists bay numbers as text. Fill the blank so they print in numeric order, from smallest to largest.

options.feedback: Right. - turns both texts into numbers and returns their difference.
Two texts are compared as text, character by character, so "10" lands before "8". The result is not in numeric order.
This sorts in numeric order, but from the largest to the smallest.
This sorts by number of characters, so 9 and 8 stay in their original order before 10.
A comparison that always says equal leaves the array in its original order.

items.explanation: The comparison function must return a negative, zero or positive number. Subtraction converts the texts to numbers, so a - b orders by numeric value from smallest to largest.
hints: Look at what the comparison function must return.
- always works on numbers, so it converts its operands.
Choose the chip that turns both texts into numbers and is negative when a is the smaller number.
